headline: Night Guard uses open AI model to monitor kids' game chats for predatory tactics
summary: With over 50,000 sextortion reports in 2025, Night Guard helps parents by highlighting potential pressure tactics in online chats, running locally on the family's computer for privacy.
details: Parents often struggle to monitor all their children's online communications. The US National Center for Missing & Exploited Children reported over 50,000 cases of financial sextortion in 2025, highlighting the urgent need for better safeguards.

Night Guard is an open-model guard designed to reduce parental review effort by highlighting possible pressure tactics in real-time. It identifies behaviors like asking a child to keep a secret, move to a private app, or send a photo.

Unlike simple bad-word filters or sentiment analysis, Night Guard uses an open model to match messages against 14 tactics documented by child-safety research from organizations like Public Safety Canada, NCMEC, and Thorn. It provides a live overlay of the 12 most recent messages.

For enhanced privacy, the real Night Guard application runs locally on the family's computer, utilizing Google's Gemma open-weight model via Ollama. This ensures chat analysis stays on the device, with optional external link inspection as a separate action.

Currently, Night Guard operates on Windows computers, reacting autonomously as messages arrive. It uses a Chrome extension for web chats (Discord web, WhatsApp Web) and a screen guard that leverages Gemma's vision capabilities.

The system has undergone rigorous testing, with 59 passing pytest tests, including regression cases and simulated tests for its link inspector. Every model answer is further checked before being presented to a child or parent.

headline_marked: [[Making Bulin 47 AI videos that look like you]] is harder than it seems: lessons from Seedance 2.5
headline: Making Bulin 47 AI videos that look like you is harder than it seems: lessons from Seedance 2.5
summary: Creating AI videos that accurately replace a person in a reference clip, like the viral Bulin 47 trend, faces significant challenges in maintaining likeness. Developers share practical lessons on improving facial resemblance and avoiding common pitfalls with t
details: The viral Bulin 47 clip, where the Dominican artist freestyles in Spain, has sparked an AI trend: people replace Bulin 47 with themselves or a friend while keeping the original scene. Developers built a tool for this and observed real user results over two weeks.

The main challenge is making the AI video truly resemble the person in the photo. This requires video editing (subject replacement) rather than image-to-video generation, using a reference clip to maintain camera movement, crowd, lighting, and rhythm.

The tool uses Seedance 2.5 in editing mode, passing the original clip as a video reference and the user's photo as an image reference. An early hurdle was audio, as models refused clips with original sound; the fix was to send a silent reference and remux audio later.

Accurate subject replacement also requires precise prompting. Instead of simply saying "replace the man," describing the target by position and clothing, like "the performer in the open pale-pink shirt, standing behind the person holding the portable speaker," proved more effective.

Another issue arose with faces: Bulin 47 wears dark sunglasses, and when the AI removed them, eyes often appeared closed or unnatural. A specific prompt line, "His eyes are clearly open and natural, with normal blinking, looking at the camera and the crowd," largely resolved this.

The most common complaint about poor likeness stemmed from users uploading full-body photos. With the face occupying only 5-10% of the image width, the model lacked sufficient facial pixels, leading it to fill gaps with the original performer's features.

To combat this, the solution involves asking for clear, high-resolution, chest-up photos without sunglasses. The tool now auto-crops faces to chest-up before sending and also sends a square close-up of the face as a second reference image to improve likeness.

Finally, prompt wording significantly impacts results. Moving from negative instructions like "do not blend the original performer" to positive descriptions, such as "His face matches [Image2] exactly: the same face shape, eyes, eyebrows, nose, lips, jawline," yielded much better facial recognition.
